title: Why We Stay Afraid - Nautilus
gist: US and Chinese neuroscientists, publishing in Neuron, identified a mouse brain region next to the amygdala—the amygdalostriatal transition zone (ASt)—whose neurons fire longer and stronger than the amygdala's, explaining how fear responses persist after threats pass.

insights.claim: Amygdala neurons fire only briefly when an animal is first startled, leaving unexplained how fear responses are sustained.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Background mechanism relevant to anxiety/PTSD therapeutics.
insights.quote: The nerve cells in this region of the brain only fire briefly when an animal, human or otherwise, is first startled. Then they quit.

insights.claim: A newly identified region in male mice, the amygdalostriatal transition zone (ASt), fires with far more power and duration than the amygdala in response to fear and talks directly to the striatum, offering an explanation for lingering fear.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: A new circuit target could inform drug development for anxiety and PTSD.
insights.quote: Neurons in this region fire with far more power and duration in response to a fear signal than neurons in the amygdala do

insights.claim: The ASt discovery came from a joint team of neuroscientists from the United States and China, notable amid broader scientific decoupling.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: US-China research collaboration continues in basic neuroscience.
